pr_body:
implement a simple change optimization for histograms using min and max aggregations. The optimization is not applied if the range cutoff would be too small compared to the overall range from previous checkpoints. At least 20% must be cut compared to former checkpoints.

fixes #63801

The histogram case is tough, depending on the meaning of the value. If the value is a metric value it might not make sense to optimize this case as the range might be spread across the full range for all checkpoints. If the number is a case or issue number, I think terms should be used.

The most common scenario I am aware of is a monotonic increasing sequence number generated externally. For this case, the optimization should yield good results. I kept it simple, the change collector only remembers values in memory, so the transform has to run some checkpoints until it kicks in.

issue_context.title: [Transform] Continuous: Optimize change collection for histogram
issue_context.body:
#63315 introduced an optimization for `date_histogram` if the field used is different to the one used for `sync`. 

In the same way `histogram` should be optimized.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7126422/96261396-b1705a80-0fc0-11eb-965f-155af5650d10.png)

review_comments: Is `queryForChanges` only called for optimized collectors?

The indexer calls `queryForChanges` to find out if the indexer should go into change collection mode or not. If so, the transform runs "optimized". Note, this is for 1 out of potentially more than one field collector. At least one collector has to return true.

However, if `queryForChanges` returns `false`, it does _not_ mean, the transform isn't optimized:

 - if a `date_histogram` is used and the field for `sync` and the `date_histogram` is the same, the checkpoint information is used to _optimize_ the query, `queryForChanges` returns `false`, but `isOptimized` returns `true`.
 - same as above for `latest`, it's optimized, but `queryForChanges` returns `false`

I made some benchmarks and saw that the new "optimized version" runs slower if the range does not cut anything(not dramatically slower, but slower). But I have no evidence that `20%` is the perfect value here. It's highly data dependent, probably there is no perfect answer, 20% seemed reasonable.
